content: Insecticides with a molecular mass greater than 500 and an octanol/water partition coefficient (log P OW) less than -1 or greater than 4 are typically assigned a default dermal absorption value of 10%. This is based on evidence showing that the dermal absorption of certain pyrethrins and pyrethroids is approximately 1%. Therefore, it is more appropriate to use a default value of 10% rather than 100% for these compounds when specific chemical data is unavailable. However, if specific data for a pyrethroid exists, it should take precedence over the default value. A similar approach can be applied to other pesticide groups. For example, for mixtures with active ingredient concentrations above 5%, a default dermal absorption value of 25% is used, while for concentrations of 5% or less, a default of 75% is applied (EFSA, 2012). In the absence of high-quality data on dermal absorption of dry insecticides deposited on the skin or transferred from surfaces, the higher estimate of the active ingredient (concentrated or diluted) is used (EFSA, 2011, 2014). For diluted solutions, operators may be exposed to both the diluted product and the undiluted formulation. A range of toxicity tests is typically required for pesticide approval. These include: Toxicokinetic studies: Conducted in rats using single and repeated oral dosing to provide information on absorption, metabolism, distribution, and excretion of the parent compound and its metabolites. Acute toxicity studies: These define approximate lethal doses via oral, dermal, or inhalation routes and assess effects on body weight, clinical signs, and gross pathology at lower dose levels following single-dose administration. Skin and eye irritation, as well as skin sensitization studies, are also included. Repeat-dose oral toxicity studies: Conducted over a minimum of 90 days in rats and dogs to identify effects on organs, tissues, blood cells, and chemical analytes in blood and urine. Repeat-dose dermal and inhalation studies: These may be required for durations of 28 or 90 days. Genetic toxicity studies: In vitro tests for gene mutation and chromosomal damage. If positive results are observed in vitro, in vivo genetic toxicity studies are also conducted. Chronic oral toxicity and carcinogenicity studies: Performed in rats and mice to assess long-term toxicity and tumor incidence. Reproductive toxicity studies: These include multigeneration studies in rats and developmental toxicity studies in rats and rabbits to evaluate effects on male and female reproductive capacity and embryonic/fetal development. Delayed neurotoxicity studies: Required for insecticides with structures related to those known to cause delayed neurotoxicity, such as organophosphates. Specialized studies: For newer substances, studies on developmental neurotoxicity, dermal penetration, and immunotoxicology may have been performed. In some cases, in vitro tests may replace whole-animal tests. The evaluation of toxicity information should be conducted by an experienced toxicologist, who assesses the range and quality of human and animal toxicity data. While all toxicity tests are useful for hazard assessment, not all may have been performed or may meet high-quality standards. Data gaps can introduce uncertainty into the assessment. In such cases, information on chemically related compounds may be helpful. Critical factors to consider include the experimental design, quality of studies, nature and severity of observed effects, dose-response relationships, and identification of no-observed-adverse-effect levels (NOAELs) and lowest-observed-adverse-effect levels (LOAELs). Insecticides meeting the criteria for carcinogenicity, mutagenicity, or reproductive toxicity categories 1A and 1B of the Globally Harmonized System (GHS) are considered highly hazardous pesticides. When multiple insecticides are used concurrently, potential interactions should be considered. Insecticides with similar mechanisms of action may produce additive toxic effects, while those with dissimilar mechanisms may have independent effects. Interactions between active ingredients and solvents in formulated products can also influence toxicity. Dose-response assessment is a critical component of hazard evaluation, used to derive health-based guidance values and assess risks. The NOAEL approach identifies a dose without appreciable adverse effects, while the benchmark dose (BMD) method calculates doses associated with specific response levels. For substances with endocrine-mediated toxicity, the dose-response curve may not be well-defined, complicating risk assessment. Uncertainty factors (UFs) are applied to account for variability and uncertainties in the data, with default UFs of 10 for interspecies differences and 10 for interindividual variability commonly used. These factors may be adjusted based on chemical-specific data. For space spraying, different reference doses or tolerable systemic doses (TSDs) may be needed depending on the insecticide type. Long-term TSDs are typically based on systemic effects observed in chronic studies and are expressed as mg per kg body weight per day. Acute reference doses (ARfDs) are derived for insecticides with significant acute toxicity, such as organophosphates and carbamates, using NOAELs from acute dosing studies and applying UFs. Higher-tier assessments with more complex methods may be required when needed.
